description: Width tiers for Visual Arts — Years 1–2
subject: Visual Arts

width_notes.minimum: The narrowest single task context that honestly meets the descriptor's command term. For Years 1–2, minimum is one making or exploring act with identifiable use of visual conventions or materials.
width_notes.typical: Full descriptor scope as intended — engagement across several materials, processes or cultural contexts with developing intentionality.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment through additional cultural contexts, materials, forms or purposes. Adds new contexts, not higher difficulty.

AC9AVA2C01.minimum_width: Use at least one visual convention (line, shape, colour, texture) and one visual arts process with chosen materials to create an artwork.
AC9AVA2C01.typical_width: Use combinations of visual conventions, processes and materials (including both analog and digital) to create artworks; make intentional choices informed by experimentation; explore mark-making, collage, printmaking, 3D construction and digital tools.
wider: Create an artwork inspired by First Nations Australian visual arts and designs — explore colours, symbols or patterns with culturally authoritative resources or community representatives
Combine digital and analog art-making to create a collaged abstract work that responds to sensory input (e.g. music, texture) and communicates feelings or emotions
Use nature-printing or collagraph techniques to create prints that explore texture and surface, extending understanding of how materials produce visual effects
elaborations: using a combination of chaotic/accidental mark-making with more detailed intentional mark-making; for example, using blobs of paint with added outlines and detail, and using imagination and creativity to build on the shapes to see what emerges

using Viewpoints to develop questions as they experiment with arrangement and rearrangement to shuffle visual conventions, subject matter and materials around a designated area and to deliberately change the meaning of a visual story; for example,
or
using visual brainstorming to build ideas for artworks and using Viewpoints to develop questions to push ideas further; for example,

creating a relief print through nature-printing, or creating collagraphs by creating a raised textured surface by using glue, thread/string and textured paper to create monoprints; cutting these shapes out and making a collage to create a recognisable form, such as a face or an animal

using 3D construction (sculpture) methods to represent subject matter or ideas being explored in another learning area; for example, building on their understanding of living things as a starting point to use modelling materials such as potato clay and found objects to represent the life cycle of an insect

using a combination of digital art and analog art-making, such as using photography or drawing apps for painting and drawing, to create a collaged abstract work that represents feelings and emotions; for example, responding with colour, line and shape to music to create work that communicates how the music makes them feel

AC9AVA2D01.minimum_width: Experiment with one material or process to discover a new possibility; share what was discovered or what failed.
AC9AVA2D01.typical_width: Experiment with a range of materials and processes; explore visual conventions through play, limitation and layering; use Viewpoints questions to reflect on discoveries; document thinking and learning.
wider: Explore visual conventions used in artworks and designs created by First Nations Australians — identify colours, symbols and patterns with guidance from culturally authoritative resources
Use digital tools (photography, drawing apps) to go on a 'line hunt' — identify, capture and categorise different types of lines found in the school environment
Explore layering as a visual technique — build a 'layer + layer + layer' surface using mixed media (pastels, watercolour, ink, wax) and reflect on how each material contributes
elaborations: playing with a range of natural and/or constructed materials to experiment with visual conventions and visual arts processes; for example, creating mud sculptures, or using sticks, leaves and playdough to explore texture

unpacking a surprise bag of everyday tools and materials, and working silently in small groups to make something within limitations; for example, using materials of only one colour or making sculptural forms from paper or cardboard using only folding and tearing processes
using Viewpoints to develop questions to reflect on their arts experiences; for example,

identifying the difference between open lines and closed shapes; digitally filling a selection or colour block using a collage of closed shapes to form silhouettes of recognisable objects, people or other living things
examining artworks and trialling

as a way of building surfaces, colour, texture and interest; for example, experimenting to create a layered world with pastels, then watercolour, ink and wax, and once the experiment is completed, identifying how each material could be used in a future artwork
exploring visual conventions using a wide range of materials; for example, creating lines using media such as pastels, chalk, paint, ripped paper, textiles and markers; or going on a
to identify and photograph the different lines they see around their school environment using a digital camera, or creating rubbings

AC9AVA2E01.minimum_width: Explore one artwork or visual arts practice from a culture, community or context different from their own; share one observation or question about it.
AC9AVA2E01.typical_width: Explore a range of artworks by living Australian artists and artworks from different cultures, communities and contexts; use Viewpoints questions to investigate artists and their practices; compare subject matter, materials and purposes.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian visual arts, crafts and designs — explore when, where and why these are used to share cultural knowledge, including during significant occasions such as NAIDOC Week or Reconciliation Week, using culturally authoritative resources
Explore artworks that represent significant events from different times (celebrations, living things and their environments) and identify similarities and differences across cultural contexts
Explore artworks by local First Nations Australian artists from a regional, state or national collection — discuss what the artwork might communicate and what questions you would ask the artist
elaborations: investigating a diverse range of artworks made by living Australian artists; for example, artworks from a local, national, state or regional collection

exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use visual arts, crafts and designs to share knowledge about cultures; for example, during celebrations such as Aboriginal Children's Week, NAIDOC week, Reconciliation Week or to acknowledge significant occasions such as Sorry Day
using Viewpoints to co-develop questions to explore and investigate ideas and understandings about artworks, craft works or designs; for example,
using Viewpoints to co-develop questions to explore an artist and their practice; for example,

identifying similarities and differences in artworks that represent subject matter or ideas they may be exploring in other learning areas; for example, exploring artworks that represent significant events from different times such as celebrations, or subject matter such as living creatures and their relationships with their environment

AC9AVA2E02.minimum_width: Explore one artwork or design created by a First Nations Australian artist; share one observation about how it represents place, culture or identity.
AC9AVA2E02.typical_width: Explore artworks by First Nations Australian artists that feature Country/Place as central to identity; investigate visual conventions (colours, symbols, patterns) with guidance from culturally authoritative resources; listen to First Nations artists' own voices about the importance of art-making.
wider: Explore artworks that represent First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky — co-create symbols and designs to represent shapes and patterns seen at different times of year with First Nations Australians who have cultural authority
Observe how First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear in community and national events — identify how artists observe protocols and respect Elders or knowledge holders
Investigate how First Nations Australian artists use visual arts to show that where we are is part of who we are — examine artworks that connect identity to specific Country/Place
elaborations: exploring how artworks created by First Nations Australian artists feature places as a way to show us why where we are is a part of who we are

identifying where they might experience First Nations Australians' cultural expressions in their lives and communities and as part of state and national events, taking notice of ways that artists observe protocols and respect Elders or knowledge holders

listening to the voices of First Nations Australian artists as they describe the importance of Country/Place to their art-making; for example, through direct engagement or using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

observing how visual conventions are used in artworks and designs created by First Nations Australians; for example, exploring colours, symbols and patterns used in artworks with representatives of the First Nations Australian community or through resources that are created or co-created by First Nations Australians

exploring artworks that represent First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky, co-creating symbols and/or designs to represent shapes and patterns that can be seen at different times of the year with First Nations Australians who have cultural authority

AC9AVA2P01.minimum_width: Share one artwork with a peer, small group or teacher in an informal setting; say something about what they like or what they made.
AC9AVA2P01.typical_width: Share artworks and arts practice in multiple informal settings — presenting to the class, posting on a school learning management system, participating in peer matching or discussion activities; explain choices, processes and ideas.
wider: Perform or dramatise the making of a work — use gesture and movement to communicate the creative process, then select the most successful section and frame it for display
Share a work-in-progress with peers and explain decisions made so far — what the work communicates and what might change
Create an everyday-object artwork (drawing an object and personifying it) and share with the class as a guessing game — explain how they arrived at their interpretation
elaborations: presenting an artwork they have made to the class, a small group or their teacher and explaining what they like about it
